Header:
Date: 2026-05-28 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya (CTO OpenHealthcare), Carlos (Platform Eng), Jenna (ML Eng)
---
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — priya will run through the runtime deep dive, we can stop for questions. jenna, maya, carlos from OpenHealthcare, right?
[00:06] Jenna: yep hi all. thanks for setting this up. we pulled together some sample EHR exports to demo.
[00:10] Priya: great. i want to start with the high level: our long-context runtime supports up to 128k tokens in production today with specific optimizations around kv cache, attention tiling, and chunking. we'll go into numbers — latency/throughput tradeoffs — but first any constraints we should know?
[00:20] Maya: data residency and HIPAA-ish compliance are big. we need VPC + CMEK, audit logs, and clarity on on-prem options if required. also cost is a concern.
[00:28] Alex: noted. we'll cover private deployment and KMS stuff later. priya take it away.
[00:32] Priya: ok jumping in. (mild background) first principle: serving 128k contexts is mostly about memory and kv cache management. we stream the KV cache across sequence chunks and we use a tiled attention kernel when sequences exceed the typical 4k/32k sweet spots. that means we avoid quadratic blowup by slicing attention into blocks — less VM memory spikes.
[00:55] Priya: quick caveat: "KV cache" in some transcripts becomes "K V cash" ; sorry the auto-transcript can be messy.
[01:02] Carlos: can you clarify how you shard the KV cache? is it per-request or shared across requests?
[01:08] Priya: good q. per-request logical KV — we persist a compressed form on the host process and spill to a fast NVMe cache if the in-memory LRU evicts. for long-context workloads we recommend pinned Dedicated instance groups so the hot KV stays memory-resident. if you run hosted multi-tenant, we do transparent spilling but there is a latency tail when fetching from NVMe.
[01:28] Jenna: how big are the spills? on our data a single patient history can be 40-60k tokens.
[01:35] Priya: typical token-to-bytes depends on model and tokenizer, but rough rule: 128k tokens ~ 600-750MB in float16 KV. with quantized KV we can drop that to ~200-300MB. so yeah 40-60k is significant but fits in memory on a 32-48GB GPU if you use quantized kernels and memory-optimized runtime.
[01:54] Maya: you mentioned quantized KV. i'm worried about quality regression for clinical summarization. what have you seen?
[02:02] Priya: good point. quantization of KV (and weights) can slightly change logits ordering in edge cases — we've got a few levers. 1) use mixed quantization: activations/kv in int8 while keeping final layers in float16. 2) run evals on your prompt set — we do an A/B on accuracy/ROUGE depending on task. often cost/latency win is worth it but we avoid quant on critical steps unless metrics show parity.
[02:30] Alex: side note — Redwood Optimize can suggest per-route quant profiles based on observed prompts.
[02:36] Carlos: what about chunking strategies? do you recommend overlapping windows or hierarchical chunking?
[02:41] Priya: we commonly use a hybrid: chunk + retrieval + overlap. for 128k we slice into ~16k windows with 1-2k overlap and maintain a persistent prefix cache for the most recent tokens. overlap helps reduce attention discontinuities but increases compute. hierarchical is great for retrieval-augmented tasks: compress older chunks into summaries and keep only the most relevant dense vectors for retrieval.
[03:04] Jenna: that sounds like extra engineering on our side. can Redwood handle the chunking + stitching?
[03:09] Priya: yes, we provide client-side helpers and server-side stitching primitives. you can stream partial KV updates back to the runtime. we also offer an offline preprocessor for chunking + dense-vector index creation.
[03:20] [03:21] Maya: latency numbers — give us an example for a 64k seq vs 128k seq on dedicated vs hosted please.
[03:26] Priya: rough benchmarks: on Dedicated A100-like instance with optimized kernels: 64k generation (200 tokens output) median latency ~1.1s per 1k output tokens (so ~220ms per 200-token response) — those numbers are highly workload dependent. 128k has larger KV overhead — median add ~30-40% latency unless you use overlapping/streaming prefix. Hosted multi-tenant will add additional tail from scheduling and NVMe spills — expect 1.5x to 2.5x in 95th percentile.
[03:54] Alex: to clarify — those numbers assume batching disabled for low-latency interactive use. if you batch, throughput improves but P95 latency suffers.
[04:02] Carlos: can you explain batching tradeoffs for our throughput needs? we expect peaks during batch ingest windows.
[04:08] Priya: sure — continuous batching is our runtime's approach: small micro-batches coalesced, respecting latency SLOs. for offline batch jobs (e.g., vectorizing thousands of documents) you can push large batches for best GPU efficiency. For interactive clinical summarization, keep batch size small and use Dedicated to avoid noisy neighbors.
[04:25] Jenna: is there an autoscale approach for Dedicated clusters? we don't want to overcommit GPUs.
[04:30] Alex: yes Dedicated supports autoscaling with cold/warm pools and burst capacity we can preconfigure; cost optimized. you can set a scale policy tied to queue depth and latency targets.
[04:40] [04:41] Maya: let's talk security: if we go Private/VPC with CMEK, can we still use the optimizer features?
[04:47] Priya: yes — in Private deployments we ship the inference runtime and the Optimize/observability agents talk back to your control plane over mutual TLS only if you opt in. CMEK/HSM for keys is supported; audit logs and SAML SSO are standard. you'll still get the profiling data we need for cost suggestions without moving customer data to our hosted service.
[05:05] Carlos: on-prem is attractive. what's the ops burden? we run k8s on-prem already.
[05:10] Priya: our on-prem package integrates with k8s (helm charts) and uses node selectors for GPU types. we provide prebuilt kernels optimized for common GPUs, but you may need kernel tuning for very custom hardware. support tier includes runbook reviews and a one-time setup consultancy.
[05:25] Jenna: any thoughts on attention optimizations? we saw some papers on sparse attention and chunked attention.
[05:30] Priya: yes. we use a mix: for extremely long contexts we switch to a block-sparse attention kernel and rotary/ALiBi position encodings to maintain relative position efficiency. Also KV caching avoids recomputing prior attention. For retrieval-heavy workflows, we bias attention toward recent windows using causal masks and importance weighting to reduce compute.
[05:50] [05:51] Maya: do you support custom model variants? we already fine-tuned an LLM for clinical language.
[05:56] Priya: absolutely. we can onboard your fine-tuned checkpoint — we do a quick compatibility pass, quantization safety checks, and per-route profiling. some custom ops may need custom kernels but we can usually fallback to slower but correct execution while we optimize.
[06:12] Alex: quick interruption—jenna, can you share a sanitized sample of what a patient thread looks like? we'll use that for the benchmark.
[06:18] Jenna: yes i'll upload a redacted export to the S3 link after this call. should be ~10 patients to start.
[06:24] Priya: perfect. our benchmark template will run inference with your real prompt patterns and record latency, token cost, and quality metrics (F1/ROUGE where applicable).
[06:33] Carlos: regarding monitoring — what metrics will we get? token-level cost, latency percentiles, KV hit/miss?
[06:39] Priya: all of the above. Console exposes token-level breakdown, KV cache hit ratio, memory utilization, per-route P50/P95/P99 latencies, and ingest queue depth. We can also stream traces into your Datadog / Grafana.
[06:51] [06:52] Alex: moving toward next steps — we'll run the benchmark, share results, and then sync on deployment mode (Dedicated vs Private). any blockers?
[06:58] Maya: just compliance review on the security pack. also we need an estimated TCO for Dedicated vs Private for our projected load.
[07:05] Alex: we'll include a sample TCO sheet.
[07:09] Priya: i'll kick off the benchmark once jenna uploads data and will send a quick runbook for dataset formatting.
[07:14] Jenna: plan to upload today. one more question — do you support model fallbacks if a large request times out?
[07:20] Priya: yes — our smart routing supports auto-fallback to a smaller/quantized model or to a shorter-context variant and we can stitch results. configurable per-route.
[07:29] Carlos: any considerations about tokenization differences for clinical text? e.g., long ICD codes?
[07:35] Priya: tokenizer affects token counts; we recommend using the same tokenizer as your fine-tuned model and including tokenization in the pre-benchmark. often medically dense text tokenizes more compactly than verbose prose, but check hat. (laugh)
[07:48] Alex: ok wrapping — recap: 1) Jenna uploads sanitized dataset; 2) Priya runs 128k benchmark and shares results by 2026-06-04; 3) Alex sends pricing/security docs by 2026-05-31; 4) follow-up meeting week of 2026-06-08.
[07:59] Maya: sounds good, thanks.
[08:01] Jenna: thanks team.
[08:02] Alex: thanks all — we'll follow up in email.
